title: Debugging toolbox
scopeHtml: Scope: top, vmstat, iostat, strace, lsof, ss, perf, flame graphs and a worked incident.

notes.title: A method before the tools
notes.html:
Debugging a slow or broken Linux server is a search problem: narrow from "something is wrong" to one resource, then one process, then one function. Tools are easy; the order is what interviewers test.

Brendan Gregg's USE method: for every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network), check Utilisation (how busy), Saturation (queued work waiting) and Errors. Saturation is the key signal: a resource at 100% with a queue is a bottleneck; at 60% with no queue, it is not.

The first 60 seconds on a sick box (from Netflix's public checklist):

uptime                 # load averages: trend over 1, 5, 15 min
dmesg -T | tail        # OOM kills, disk errors, NIC resets
vmstat 1               # run queue, swap, cpu split
mpstat -P ALL 1        # per-CPU: one hot core?
pidstat 1              # per-process CPU
iostat -xz 1           # disk latency and saturation
free -m                # memory (look at available)
sar -n DEV 1           # network throughput
sar -n TCP,ETCP 1      # retransmits, resets
top                    # overview

Worked example. Report: "checkout is slow". You do not guess; you ask: is the host CPU-bound (vmstat r > cores), memory-bound (si/so non-zero, available low), disk-bound (iostat await high, %util near 100), network-bound (retransmits), or is the app waiting on a downstream (all idle but threads blocked)? Each tool below answers one of those.

Industry examples. Netflix's performance team and Brendan Gregg's books (Systems Performance, BPF Performance Tools) popularised USE and flame graphs. Google SRE's "four golden signals" (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) are the application-level cousin.

Everyday analogy. A doctor does vitals first (pulse, temperature), then focuses on the organ, and only then orders the expensive scan.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to perf or a profiler before checking if the machine is even the problem.
  • Looking at utilisation only and missing saturation (queues).
  • Changing five things at once, so nothing can be attributed.

notes.title: top, load average and uptime
notes.html:
Load average is the average number of tasks that are running or waiting to run (and on Linux also those in uninterruptible I/O sleep, state D). It is shown by uptime for 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare with the core count: load 8 on 8 cores is full; load 8 on 32 cores is mostly idle.

$ uptime
 14:02:11 up 41 days,  3:12,  2 users,  load average: 18.40, 12.10, 6.30
$ nproc
8

Rising 1-minute above 15-minute means getting worse. Because Linux counts D-state tasks, a high load with idle CPU usually means I/O wait or lock waits, not CPU use.

$ top -b -n1 | head -15
top - 14:02:11 up 41 days,  load average: 18.40, 12.10, 6.30
Tasks: 312 total,  11 running, 301 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
%Cpu(s): 21.0 us,  9.0 sy,  0.0 ni, 10.0 id, 58.0 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.5 si,  1.5 st
MiB Mem :  31900 total,    410 free,   9100 used,  22390 buff/cache
MiB Swap:   2048 total,   2048 free,      0 used.  22400 avail Mem
  PID USER  PR NI    VIRT    RES   SHR S %CPU %MEM  COMMAND
 2310 app   20  0 9217344 3.1g 28344 S 140.0 10.0 java

How to read the CPU line:

Field Meaning Worry when
us User code Near 100%: compute-bound, profile it
sy Kernel work (syscalls, networking) High (over 30%): syscall heavy, lock contention, packet storm
wa Idle, but waiting on disk I/O Sustained high: storage bottleneck
st Stolen by the hypervisor Over 5%: noisy neighbour on the VM
si/hi Interrupts One core at 100% si: NIC interrupt imbalance
id Idle

Process columns: VIRT (address space, mostly irrelevant), RES (resident RAM), SHR (shared), process state S sleeping, R running, D uninterruptible disk wait (cannot be killed; many D tasks = stuck storage/NFS), Z zombie (parent did not wait). In top press 1 for per-CPU, H for per-thread, M sort by memory, P by CPU. %CPU over 100 means multiple cores.

Pressure Stall Information (PSI, kernel 4.20+) is the best single signal: cat /proc/pressure/cpu, /proc/pressure/memory, /proc/pressure/io. some avg10=40 means that for 40% of the last 10 s at least one task was stalled waiting on that resource. This is saturation measured directly.

Industry examples. Facebook's oomd uses PSI to kill workloads before the kernel OOM killer; Android's lmkd uses PSI as well.

Everyday analogy. Load average is the length of the queue at a bank including people waiting for the vault (disk); a long queue with idle tellers means the vault is the problem.

Common interview traps.

  • Reading load average as CPU percent. On Linux it includes disk waiters.
  • Panicking at high buff/cache memory. It is reclaimable.
  • Missing that top hides per-thread detail until you press H.

notes.title: vmstat and memory
notes.html:
vmstat 1 prints one line per second covering the run queue, memory, swap, I/O, interrupts and CPU split. The first line is the average since boot; ignore it.

$ vmstat 1 5
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
 3  0      0 812304 120044 2210032    0    0     0     4 9120 8100 38  9 52  1  0   healthy
14  2 481024  20120   4012  180022 4400 5100  9100 12000 22000 90000 12 20  5 63  0  swapping

Columns that matter:

  • r: runnable tasks. Persistently above the number of cores means CPU saturation.
  • b: tasks blocked in uninterruptible sleep (I/O). Above zero for long means storage stalls.
  • si / so: pages swapped in and out per second. Any sustained non-zero so means memory pressure; a service doing real swap work is typically already in trouble (latency x100).
  • bi / bo: blocks in and out of devices.
  • in / cs: interrupts and context switches per second. 100k+ cs with modest CPU often points to lock contention or tiny packet handling.
  • wa: iowait.

Complementary tools:

$ free -m
              total  used  free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:          31900  9100   410     120       22390      22400    # available is what matters
$ sar -B 1                    # paging stats: majflt/s (major faults reading from disk), pgscand/s (direct reclaim)
$ cat /proc/meminfo | grep -E 'MemAvailable|Slab|AnonPages|Dirty'
$ slabtop -o | head           # kernel memory (dentries, inodes) when 'used' grows but processes don't
$ smem -tk -c 'pid name pss'  # PSS: fair per-process memory with shared pages split
$ ps aux --sort=-rss | head -5

Key ideas: RSS (resident), PSS (proportional shared), page cache reclaimable, swap to a disk (cliffs in latency), OOM killer chooses a victim by oom_score (/proc/PID/oom_score; oom_score_adj -1000 protects a process). dmesg -T | grep -i oom shows the verdict. Transparent Huge Pages (THP) compaction can cause latency spikes in databases; many (Redis, MongoDB, Oracle) advise never or madvise.

Worked example. free shows 410 MB free but 22 GB available: healthy. so > 0 for minutes and majflt/s high: genuine pressure. Slab growing to 8 GB with dentry cache: a program creating millions of files or lookups of non-existent paths.

Industry examples. Redis forks for snapshots (RDB/AOF rewrite); copy-on-write can double memory use under write load. That is a classic "worked fine until the snapshot ran" OOM, so keep headroom (vm.overcommit_memory=1, enough free RAM).

Everyday analogy. Desk and filing cabinet: swap is when the desk overflows and papers go to a basement; every lookup becomes a trip downstairs.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "free memory is low, so add RAM". Check available, swap activity, and major faults.
  • Adding swap to "fix" a leak: it delays the symptom and degrades latency.

notes.title: iostat and disk bottlenecks
notes.html:
iostat -x shows each block device's throughput, queue and latency. The sysstat package. Use -x for extended stats, -z to hide idle devices, -d 1 to repeat every second.

$ iostat -xz 1
Device  r/s    w/s   rkB/s   wkB/s  r_await w_await aqu-sz rareq-sz  %util
nvme0n1 450.0 2900.0 7200.0 185000.0    0.9    18.4   53.2     16.0  99.8
sda      12.0    5.0   480.0    200.0    8.2     9.0    0.2     40.0   3.1

How to read it:

  • r_await, w_await (ms): average time a request spends queued plus serviced. Healthy NVMe: under 1 ms. Healthy SATA SSD: 1 to 2 ms. HDD: 5 to 15 ms. Cloud network disks (EBS gp3): 1 to 5 ms typical.
  • aqu-sz: average queue length. A sustained value above 1 for an HDD (or above the device's useful parallelism) means saturation.
  • %util: fraction of time with at least one request in flight. Misleading for NVMe and arrays, which handle many in parallel: 100% does not always mean no headroom. Use latency plus queue size to judge.
  • rareq-sz/wareq-sz: average request size; tiny sizes (4 KB) with high IOPS means random I/O.
  • IOPS = r/s + w/s; throughput = rkB/s + wkB/s. Compare against the device or cloud limit (for AWS EBS gp3 baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s; provisioned IOPS io2 for more; credit-based gp2/burst balances can run out).
$ sudo iotop -oPa                        # accumulate I/O per process (only active)
$ pidstat -d 1                           # kB_rd/s kB_wr/s per process, no root needed for own procs
$ sudo biolatency-bpfcc 10 1             # BCC: latency histogram of block I/O
     usecs     : count   distribution
       128 -> 255   : 112390 |*************  |
      8192 -> 16383 :   8210 |*             |   <- the slow tail
$ sudo biosnoop-bpfcc                    # every I/O with PID, size, latency

Worked example. w_await 18 ms with aqu-sz 53 and %util 99.8 on an NVMe that normally answers in 0.1 ms: saturated by a heavy writer (log flood or backup). pidstat -d points to the culprit logrotate/rsync; ionice -c3 and nice demote it. Cure may be spreading writes (the writeback flood in the file system note), or buying IOPS.

Industry examples. Cloud incidents often come from exceeding the provisioned IOPS/throughput of a volume or running out of burst credits, not from a "broken" disk. Databases publish "fsync latency" and "checkpoint" metrics as early warnings.

Everyday analogy. A single cashier line: aqu-sz is the queue length, await is how long you waited in total, and %util is how often the cashier was busy.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating %util 100% as definitive on NVMe or RAID.
  • Ignoring request size and pattern: 10,000 IOPS of 4 KB is 40 MB/s, trivial throughput but possibly a hit IOPS limit.
  • Blaming the app when the same volume is shared with a backup job.

notes.title: strace, lsof and ss
notes.html:
strace shows system calls a process makes; lsof shows open files and sockets; ss shows sockets and their queues. They answer "what is this process actually doing?" without source code.

strace.

$ sudo strace -f -tt -T -p 2310 -e trace=network,file 2>&1 | head
14:02:11.120 connect(14, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(5432), sin_addr=10.0.3.7}, 16) = 0 <0.000321>
14:02:11.121 sendto(14, "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ...", 74, 0, NULL, 0) = 74 <0.000012>
14:02:13.330 recvfrom(14, "\0\0\1...", 8192, 0, NULL, NULL) = 4096 <2.209114>   # 2.2 s waiting on DB!
$ sudo strace -c -f -p 2310 -- sleep 10       # summary table by syscall
% time     seconds  usecs/call  calls  errors syscall
 62.10    4.920000        1240   3968     812 futex
 20.30    1.610000         410   3900       0 epoll_wait
$ strace -e trace=openat -f ./myprog 2>&1 | grep ENOENT     # which config files does it look for?

Useful flags: -f follow threads/children, -T time spent in each call, -tt timestamps, -e trace=... filter (file, network, process, memory), -c summary, -s 200 longer strings. Warning: strace uses ptrace and can slow the target by 10 to 100 times; on a busy production process use perf trace or bpftrace/strace -c for short windows only.

lsof.

$ lsof -p 2310 | wc -l                         # open fd count vs ulimit
$ lsof -i :8080                                # who listens/uses port 8080
COMMAND  PID USER  FD  TYPE NODE NAME
java    2310 app   45u IPv6 TCP *:8080 (LISTEN)
$ lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:ESTABLISHED | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
$ lsof +L1                                     # deleted files still held open (space leak)
$ ls /proc/2310/fd | wc -l ; grep 'open files' /proc/2310/limits

Fd leaks look like a slowly rising ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l until EMFILE: Too many open files. lsof -p PID then shows thousands of the same socket or file.

ss (replaces netstat).

$ ss -s                                  # totals by state
$ ss -tnp state established '( dport = :5432 )' | wc -l    # connections to Postgres
$ ss -ltn                                # LISTEN sockets: Recv-Q = accept queue depth, Send-Q = backlog size
$ ss -ti dst 10.0.3.7                    # per connection TCP internals: rtt, cwnd, retrans
   cubic wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:1.2/0.6 cwnd:10 bytes_retrans:5840 retrans:0/4
$ ss -tn state time-wait | wc -l         # port exhaustion check
$ nstat -az | grep -E 'Retrans|ListenOverflows|ListenDrops'

Industry examples. "strace showed 40,000 stat() calls per request" is a recurring story (config reloaded on each request, or a library walking the path). strace -c summaries often reveal that an app is mostly in futex (lock contention) or epoll_wait (waiting, idle).

Everyday analogy. strace is listening to every phone call a person makes; lsof is looking at what is on their desk; ss is checking the state of each open line.

Common interview traps.

  • Attaching strace -f to a hot production service and making the outage worse.
  • Reading a long epoll_wait as a problem; it means idle, which is good.
  • Forgetting ss -ltn Recv-Q on a listener to detect overload of the accept queue.

notes.title: perf, profiling and flame graphs
notes.html:
perf samples what the CPUs are executing, many times per second, and tells you where the time goes. A sampling profiler takes a stack trace every N microseconds (for example 99 Hz, an odd number to avoid lock-step with timers). Hot functions appear in many samples.

$ sudo perf top -p 2310                         # live: which functions burn CPU
  22.40%  libjvm.so   [.] G1ParScanThreadState::trim_queue
  14.10%  [kernel]    [k] _raw_spin_lock
   9.80%  libc.so.6   [.] __memcpy_avx_unaligned
$ sudo perf record -F 99 -g -p 2310 -- sleep 30     # record with call stacks for 30 s
$ sudo perf report --no-children | head -30
$ sudo perf stat -p 2310 -- sleep 10
   2,841,201,114  cycles ;  1,102,883,010  instructions   # IPC 0.39 = mostly stalled on memory
       182,044  context-switches ;   12,100 cpu-migrations ;   4,400 page-faults

IPC (instructions per cycle) hints: below about 1 means stalled waiting on memory; above 2 means compute-bound. For managed languages, you need symbols: Java -XX:+PreserveFramePointer and perf-map-agent (or async-profiler), Node --perf-basic-prof, Go has frame pointers by default.

Flame graphs (Brendan Gregg) show the sampled stacks as stacked boxes: the x axis is the share of samples (not time order), the y axis is stack depth, width = how often a function (and its children) was on-CPU. Look for the wide plateaus at the top: that is where the CPU is actually spent.

git clone https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph
sudo perf record -F 99 -g -p 2310 -- sleep 30
sudo perf script | ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl | ./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > cpu.svg
 main
 |-- handleRequest ---------------------------------- 100%
     |-- parseJson ---------- 15%
     |-- priceLookup ---------------------------- 60%     <- wide: investigate
         |-- regexMatch -------------------- 52%         <- wider: the hot spot
     |-- writeResponse ---- 10%

Other flame graph types: off-CPU flame graphs (where threads block: locks, I/O; built with bpftrace/offcputime-bpfcc) answer "why is it slow while CPU is low"; differential flame graphs compare before/after a deploy. Tools: async-profiler (Java, low overhead, also lock and allocation modes), py-spy (Python without code changes), Go pprof, Parca/Pyroscope for continuous profiling, bpftrace one-liners.

# bpftrace: histogram of read() latency by process, almost no overhead
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_read { @s[tid] = nsecs; }
                  tracepoint:syscalls:sys_exit_read /@s[tid]/ { @us[comm] = hist((nsecs-@s[tid])/1000); delete(@s[tid]); }'

Decision gravity. perf and eBPF tools are low overhead (1 to 3%) and safe on production; strace and heavy tracers are not. Continuous profiling in production (Parca, Pyroscope, Google-Wide Profiling) is a cheap permanent investment.

Industry examples. Google-Wide Profiling samples every fleet machine continuously; Netflix runs flame graphs from production to find regressions; Meta publishes how a 0.5% CPU win at their scale saves a data centre's worth of servers.

Everyday analogy. Taking a photo of the shop floor every second for 30 seconds: wherever most photos show people queued is the slow desk.

Common interview traps.

  • Reading the x axis as time. It is alphabetical/merged samples, not a timeline.
  • Profiling CPU when the process is blocked (off-CPU time never shows in a CPU flame graph).
  • Missing symbols (shows hex addresses) because of omitted frame pointers or missing debuginfo.

notes.title: Worked incident: checkout latency spike
notes.html:
Alert at 14:02: p99 latency of the checkout API rose from 80 ms to 6 s. Error rate 4% (timeouts). It started 10 minutes after a deploy of a new "recommendations" feature. Service: Java 21, 8 vCPU VM, Postgres on a separate host, Redis cache.

Step 1: broad health (30 seconds).

$ uptime
 14:05:02 up 41 days,  load average: 22.10, 9.80, 4.20      # rising fast, 8 cores
$ vmstat 1 3
 r  b  swpd  free   buff  cache  si so   bi    bo   in    cs us sy id wa st
21  1     0 612304 120044 2210032  0  0  120   300 28000 96000 86 12  2  0  0

r = 21 on 8 cores: CPU saturated; wa 0 so not disk; us 86%: user code. No swap. So it is CPU-bound in user space. Disk and memory ruled out in under a minute.

Step 2: which process and threads.

$ top -H -p $(pgrep -f checkout.jar)
  PID   %CPU COMMAND
 2418   96.0 http-nio-8080-exec-3
 2421   95.3 http-nio-8080-exec-6
 2433   94.1 http-nio-8080-exec-9      # many request threads all hot: not one runaway GC thread
$ jstat -gcutil $(pgrep -f checkout.jar) 1000 3
  S0  S1   E    O    M   CCS  YGC  YGCT  FGC   FGCT
  0  80  92   61   96   88  4110 31.2    2   0.8    # young GC frequent but short; not a full GC storm

All request threads hot and GC modest: the application code itself burns CPU per request.

Step 3: profile with a flame graph (30 s, low overhead).

$ ./profiler.sh -d 30 -f /tmp/cpu.html $(pgrep -f checkout.jar)     # async-profiler

The flame graph shows 58% of samples under RecommendationService.rank() → java.util.regex.Pattern.matcher → Pattern$Branch.match (regex backtracking). The new feature builds and compiles a regex per request and runs a pattern prone to catastrophic backtracking on long product titles.

Step 4: confirm with a second angle.

$ sudo perf stat -p 2310 -- sleep 5    # IPC 2.1 = real compute, not memory stalls
$ sudo strace -c -f -p 2310 -- sleep 5 # syscalls few: not I/O; only futex on the shared regex cache
$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/http.server.requests | head   # latency split by endpoint: only /checkout/recs

Step 5: mitigate first, fix after. Feature flag the recommendations off (2 minutes): load average falls to 2.0, p99 returns to 85 ms. That is the mitigation. The fix: precompile the Pattern as a static final, replace the pattern with a possessive/linear-time one (or use RE2/java.util.regex timeouts via a bounded input), cap title length at 200 characters, add a p99 latency alert on that endpoint, and add a load test to the release checklist.

Timeline and metrics.

  • 13:52 deploy; 14:02 alert; 14:03 vmstat shows the CPU saturation; 14:08 flame graph; 14:11 flag off; 14:13 recovered. Time to mitigate: 11 minutes. Time spent guessing: zero, because each tool ruled out a resource.

Alternative diagnoses and how the same toolbox separates them.

Symptom pattern Likely cause Confirming tool
High r, us, flat flame graph top CPU-bound code (this incident) perf / async-profiler
High wa, b, await high Disk saturated iostat, iotop, biolatency
Low CPU, high cs, futex dominates Lock contention strace -c, off-CPU flame graph, jstack
so > 0, majflt high Memory pressure vmstat, sar -B, dmesg OOM
Low CPU, threads blocked in socket read Slow downstream strace -T, ss -ti, tracing
Recv-Q at backlog on LISTEN Accept queue overflow ss -ltn, nstat ListenOverflows
High st Noisy VM neighbour top, move instance
One core 100% si Interrupt imbalance /proc/interrupts, RSS/RPS tuning

Industry examples. Cloudflare's 2019 global outage was a regex with catastrophic backtracking in a WAF rule: CPU on every edge machine hit 100%. They then moved to a regex engine with linear-time guarantees and added a CPU-usage circuit breaker. Stack Overflow had an outage in 2016 from the same class of bug.

Everyday analogy. A detective works from the wide view to a single suspect, and checks alibis with different witnesses before naming the culprit.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting with "restart it" and losing the evidence. Capture thread dumps, perf, and dmesg first, or mitigate with a flag rollback.
  • Fixing the symptom (add servers) instead of the cause.
  • Not stating the difference between mitigation (stop the bleeding) and fix (remove the cause).
  • Skipping a post-incident action: alert, test, runbook.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Method: USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) per resource, then process, then function; read saturation (queues, PSI) not just percent.
  • uptime/top: load average counts runnable plus D-state tasks; split CPU into us, sy, wa, st; top -H for threads.
  • vmstat: r vs cores, b, si/so, cs; free: trust available; dmesg for OOM kills.
  • iostat -x: await, aqu-sz, request size, and device limits; iotop/pidstat -d find the process; biolatency shows the tail.
  • strace -c -T (short, costly), lsof (fd leaks, deleted files, ports), ss -ltn/-ti (accept queue, retransmits).
  • perf + flame graphs: wide boxes on top are the hot code; use off-CPU flame graphs for blocked time; bpftrace and continuous profilers are safe on production.
  • In an incident: mitigate first (flag, rollback), capture evidence, then root-cause fix, then add alert and test.

questions.promptHtml: A Linux server is "slow". How do you decide where to start, and what is the USE method?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tools are easy; the order and the discipline are what is tested.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I work from broad to narrow: one resource, then one process, then one function. The USE method says for every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network) check Utilisation (how busy), Saturation (is work queueing) and Errors. Saturation is the key signal: 100% busy with a queue is a bottleneck; 60% with no queue is not.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Symptom -> load & pressure -> which resource -> which process -> which syscall/function -> fix

First 60 seconds on a sick box:

uptime            # load trend 1/5/15 min
dmesg -T | tail   # OOM kills, disk errors, NIC resets
vmstat 1          # run queue, swap, cpu split
mpstat -P ALL 1   # one hot core?
pidstat 1         # per-process CPU
iostat -xz 1      # disk latency & saturation
free -m           # look at available
sar -n DEV 1; sar -n TCP,ETCP 1   # network, retransmits
top

Each question maps to a tool: CPU-bound (vmstat r > cores), memory-bound (si/so, low available), disk-bound (await, queue), network-bound (retransmits), or the app is waiting on a downstream. Google SRE's four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) are the application-level cousin.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Jumping to a profiler before checking whether the host is the problem.
  • Looking at utilisation only and missing queues.
  • Changing five things at once so nothing can be attributed.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a saturation signal for memory? -> Swap activity, major faults, PSI memory pressure.
  2. What for a disk? -> aqu-sz and await, not just %util.
  3. What if everything is idle but users complain? -> The wait is downstream or lock-related: check thread states, ss, tracing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: runs top and guesses. Senior: has a fixed order, reads saturation not percent, ties each tool to a hypothesis and mitigates before deep-diving.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team spent 2 hours profiling code on a box whose real problem was a saturated EBS volume visible in a 10-second iostat.

questions.promptHtml: What does load average mean on Linux, and how do you interpret load average: 18.4, 12.1, 6.3 on an 8-core machine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Load average is misread constantly, especially its inclusion of I/O waiters.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Load average is the average number of tasks that are running, waiting to run, or (on Linux) in uninterruptible I/O sleep, over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. On 8 cores a load of 8 is full. 18.4/12.1/6.3 means it is rising fast and has more than twice as many tasks as cores. But because D-state tasks count, I must check whether it is CPU demand or I/O wait before deciding.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
$ uptime
 14:02:11 up 41 days, load average: 18.40, 12.10, 6.30
$ top -b -n1 | head -4
%Cpu(s): 21.0 us, 9.0 sy, 0.0 ni, 10.0 id, 58.0 wa, 0.0 hi, 0.5 si, 1.5 st
Field Meaning Worry when
us user code near 100%: profile it
sy kernel work over 30%: syscalls, locks, packet storm
wa idle waiting on disk sustained high: storage
st stolen by hypervisor over 5%: noisy neighbour
si/hi interrupts one core at 100%: NIC IRQ imbalance

Process states: R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible disk wait (cannot be killed; many D = stuck storage/NFS), Z zombie. top keys: 1 per-CPU, H threads, P/M sort. Best saturation signal: Pressure Stall Information (/proc/pressure/cpu|memory|io, kernel 4.20+): some avg10=40 means a task was stalled 40% of the last 10 s.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading load as CPU percent.
  • Panicking at high buff/cache; it is reclaimable.
  • Forgetting top -H for per-thread detail.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. High load with idle CPU? -> Tasks blocked in D state: disk or NFS waits, or lock waits.
  2. Why is the 1-min greater than the 15-min? -> Getting worse.
  3. PSI vs load? -> PSI directly measures stall time per resource; load mixes everything.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "load over cores is bad". Senior: decomposes with CPU line and states, uses PSI, and interprets the trend.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "CPU is fine but load is 40" page turned out to be a hung NFS mount with 35 processes in D state.

questions.contextHtml:
Alert: load average 22 on a 4-core database host; the application times out. Quick look:

$ uptime
 load average: 22.1, 15.0, 7.2
$ top -b -n1 | head -12
%Cpu(s):  6.0 us,  3.0 sy,  0.0 ni, 10.0 id, 80.0 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.5 si,  0.5 st
MiB Mem: 15900 total, 410 free, 3100 used, 12390 buff/cache
 PID  S %CPU COMMAND
 910  D  2.0  postgres: writer
 944  D  1.0  postgres: checkpointer
 ... 18 more postgres processes in D
$ iostat -xz 1
Device  w/s    w_await aqu-sz %util
sda     310    480.0   148.0   100.0

Red herring: a teammate says "buff/cache is 12 GB, memory is nearly full".
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what do you do first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "CPU is not the problem so ignore the load" or "add RAM". It misses that D-state processes inflate load and the disk is the bottleneck.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this local disk, SAN or cloud volume (IOPS limits)? Did a backup, checkpoint or batch start? Any disk errors in dmesg?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Find and stop the competing writer (backup, rsync), ionice -c3 it, pause batch jobs; fail over if the disk is dying.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a heavy writer saturates the device (w_await 480 ms, queue 148); (b) device degraded or throttled by the cloud provider; (c) checkpoint storm in the DB; (d) memory pressure, ruled out because buff/cache is reclaimable and swap is idle.
  4. How I'd verify: iotop -oPa / pidstat -d 1 for the writer, dmesg -T for errors, biolatency-bpfcc, cloud metrics for burst balance and IOPS limits.
  5. Root cause: Example: a nightly backup plus the DB checkpoint pushed writes past the volume's IOPS limit. Requests queue (aqu-sz 148), processes sleep in D state, which Linux counts in load average, hence load 22 with 80% iowait and almost no CPU use.
  6. Fix: Short term: throttle or reschedule the backup, ionice. Long term: provision IOPS or move backup reads to a replica, spread checkpoints (checkpoint_completion_target), separate WAL and data volumes.
  7. Prevention: Alert on await, queue size and PSI io; track cloud IOPS credits; schedule backups away from peaks.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not adding RAM or CPUs; not killing the DB (D-state processes cannot be killed and crash recovery costs time).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can you kill -9 a D-state process? -> No, it ignores signals until the I/O returns.
  • How would PSI help? -> /proc/pressure/io would show some avg10 high, a direct saturation signal.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Burst credits on a general-purpose volume ran out at 03:00 every night after a backup started, and load average spiked with no CPU activity.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: treats load as CPU, suggests more cores/RAM.
  • Hire: reads iowait/D state and iostat, finds the writer.
  • Strong hire: IOPS limit awareness, ionice, workload separation, PSI and alerts.

questions.promptHtml: How do you read a flame graph, and what are its limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Everyone shows flame graphs; few read them correctly or know what they cannot show.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A profiler samples stack traces at, say, 99 Hz and the flame graph merges them: the x axis is the share of samples (not time order), the y axis is stack depth, and width is how often a function and its children were on-CPU. I look for wide plateaus at the top: that is where CPU is actually spent. It only shows on-CPU time, so for a slow process with low CPU I need an off-CPU graph.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
sudo perf record -F 99 -g -p 2310 -- sleep 30
sudo perf script | ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl | ./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > cpu.svg
 handleRequest ------------------------------- 100%
   parseJson ---------- 15%
   priceLookup ------------------------ 60%
      regexMatch -------------------- 52%   <- wide plateau on top: hot spot
   writeResponse ---- 10%

99 Hz (odd number) avoids lockstep with 100 Hz timers. perf stat adds IPC: below about 1 the CPU is stalled on memory, above 2 compute-bound. For managed runtimes you need symbols: Java -XX:+PreserveFramePointer and perf-map-agent or async-profiler; Node --perf-basic-prof; Go has frame pointers; Python py-spy. Variants: off-CPU flame graphs (why slow while CPU low), differential flame graphs (before/after deploy).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading the x axis as time.
  • Profiling CPU when the process is blocked.
  • Hex addresses instead of names (missing symbols/frame pointers).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A flat graph with no wide plateau? -> Death by a thousand cuts or the problem is not CPU; check off-CPU and I/O.
  2. Overhead of perf? -> About 1 to 3%, safe on production; strace is not.
  3. How to compare two deploys? -> Differential flame graph.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "find the biggest box". Senior: interprets self vs total width, knows symbols and sampling caveats, and picks on-CPU vs off-CPU.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 0.5% CPU improvement found via continuous profiling saved dozens of hosts at fleet scale.

questions.contextHtml:
A monitoring alert says "memory 97% used" on a 32 GB application server and the SRE on call wants to restart the service and request a bigger instance. Output:

$ free -m
              total  used  free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:          31900  9100   410     120       22390      22400
Swap:          2048     0  2048
$ vmstat 1 5
 r b swpd free buff cache  si so  bi  bo  in  cs us sy id wa
 3 0    0 410 120 22390     0  0   0   4 9120 8100 38 9 52 1
$ sar -B 1 3     majflt/s 0.0   pgscand/s 0.0

Another host in the same fleet shows so 5,100 and majflt/s 900.
questions.promptHtml: Is this host in trouble? What would you tell the on-call and what would you check on the other host?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "97% used, add RAM." It ignores that Linux uses spare RAM for page cache.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the alert query measure (used vs available)? Is latency affected? When did usage grow?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None on this host. Fix the alert to use MemAvailable or PSI.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) this host is healthy: 22 GB of reclaimable cache; (b) the other host with sustained so and major faults has genuine pressure; (c) slab leak on either host if used grows but process RSS does not.
  4. How I'd verify: free -m available, vmstat si/so, sar -B majflt/s and pgscand/s (direct reclaim), /proc/meminfo (Slab, AnonPages, Dirty), slabtop -o, smem -tk -c 'pid name pss', dmesg -T | grep -i oom.
  5. Root cause: The alert measures used+cache; the kernel deliberately fills free RAM with page cache. Real pressure is swap activity and major faults, as on the second host, where the working set exceeds RAM and every miss reads from disk (latency x100).
  6. Fix: Change the alert to available below 10% or PSI memory some avg10. On the pressured host: find the largest PSS consumer, reduce its heap or add RAM; do not just add swap, which delays and degrades latency.
  7. Prevention: Alert on swap-out rate, major faults, OOM kills, and PSI; capacity-plan with available.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not dropping caches (echo 3 > drop_caches) as a "fix": it hurts performance and masks nothing. Not restarting a healthy service.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• used grows but no process explains it? -> Check slab (dentries/inodes), tmpfs, shared memory, kernel modules.
  • THP concerns? -> Compaction can add latency spikes for databases; many advise madvise or never.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet-wide alert on "memory used" paged for a year; replacing it with swap-out rate cut false pages by 95%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: treats cache as used; wants to add RAM.
  • Hire: uses available, si/so, major faults.
  • Strong hire: PSI, slab/PSS investigation, alert redesign and knows why swap is a cliff.

questions.promptHtml: What can you learn with strace, what are its dangers, and what do you use instead on a busy production system?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests practical judgment: strace is powerful but can cause the outage you are investigating.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: strace shows every system call a process makes with arguments, return values and time spent, so I can see which file, which connection and which wait. It uses ptrace and can slow the target 10 to 100 times, so on a hot production process I use strace -c for a few seconds, or perf trace, bpftrace or BCC tools, which have almost no overhead.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
$ sudo strace -f -tt -T -p 2310 -e trace=network,file 2>&1 | head
14:02:11.121 sendto(14, "SELECT * FROM orders...", 74, 0, NULL, 0) = 74 <0.000012>
14:02:13.330 recvfrom(14, "\0\0\1...", 8192, 0, NULL, NULL) = 4096 <2.209114>   # 2.2 s waiting on DB
$ sudo strace -c -f -p 2310 -- sleep 10
% time  seconds  usecs/call  calls  errors  syscall
 62.10  4.920000  1240       3968   812     futex
 20.30  1.610000  410        3900   0       epoll_wait
$ strace -e trace=openat -f ./myprog 2>&1 | grep ENOENT    # which files does it look for?

Flags: -f follow threads, -T per-call time, -tt timestamps, -e filter, -c summary, -s string length. Reading results: epoll_wait dominating means idle (good); futex dominating means lock contention; thousands of stat() per request is a classic config/path bug. Low-overhead alternative:

sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat { @[comm] = count(); }'

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Attaching strace -f to a hot service and making the outage worse.
  • Treating a long epoll_wait as a problem.
  • Forgetting that strace does not show CPU time spent in user space.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is strace slow? -> Two context switches (ptrace stop) per syscall per thread.
  2. How to find where a process is blocked now? -> cat /proc/PID/stack, /proc/PID/wchan, pstack/jstack.
  3. Can strace run in a container? -> Needs CAP_SYS_PTRACE; usually from the node or an ephemeral container.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "strace shows syscalls". Senior: interprets the summary, knows the cost, and uses eBPF/perf for live systems.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An engineer attached strace to a payment service during a latency issue; the 50x slowdown turned a degradation into an outage.

questions.subtopic: Disk saturation on a cloud volume
questions.contextHtml:
A log-heavy ingestion service on an EC2-like VM with a 500 GB gp3-style volume (baseline 3,000 IOPS, 125 MB/s) sees write latency spikes every few minutes. Metrics:

$ iostat -xz 1
Device   r/s   w/s    rkB/s  wkB/s   r_await w_await aqu-sz wareq-sz %util
nvme1n1   20  2980     320   11900    1.1     64.0    190    4.0     99.9
Cloud: VolumeWriteOps 3,000/s (flat line), VolumeThroughput 12 MB/s
Instance CPU 18%.

The team proposes buying a 4x bigger instance.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bottleneck, and how do you fix it cheaply?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disk is slow, upgrade the instance." The instance is not the limit; the volume's IOPS cap is.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the write pattern (fsync per message, tiny writes)? Which volume type and provisioned IOPS? Can records be batched? Is it durable data or logs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise provisioned IOPS/throughput on the volume (an online change in most clouds) for immediate relief.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) IOPS ceiling reached: 2,980 w/s matches 3,000 IOPS; (b) tiny 4 KB writes make IOPS the limiting factor, not throughput (12 MB/s of 125); (c) fsync per record; (d) noisy sharing with another job.
  4. How I'd verify: iostat request size (wareq-sz 4 KB), cloud IOPS graph flat at the limit, strace -c -e trace=fsync,write, pidstat -d 1, biosnoop.
  5. Root cause: The service issues about 3,000 tiny writes per second. IOPS is the cap, so requests queue (aqu-sz 190) and w_await rises to 64 ms. Throughput is 10% of the limit, which proves it is IOPS not bandwidth; CPU is irrelevant.
  6. Fix: Batch and coalesce writes (group commit, 64 to 256 KB buffers), append-only sequential logging, fewer fsyncs; or provision IOPS. Result: the same 12 MB/s becomes about 100 IOPS of 128 KB writes.
  7. Prevention: Alert on volume IOPS utilisation (not just %util), w_await and queue; load test with real write sizes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Batching adds latency and a loss window on crash; choose per durability needs. A bigger instance would not raise the volume cap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is %util 99.9 proof of saturation here? -> On NVMe/cloud volumes %util can be misleading; the flat IOPS line and rising queue are the proof.
  • Why not just use local NVMe? -> Faster but ephemeral; fine for caches or replicated data.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team doubled node sizes twice before noticing that the shared volume's burst balance reached zero every afternoon.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales the instance.
  • Hire: identifies IOPS vs throughput and request size.
  • Strong hire: batching/group-commit design, durability trade-offs, provisioning and alerting on the cap.

questions.contextHtml:
A service host reports No space left on device. Yet:

$ df -h /var
/dev/sda2  100G  100G   0 100% /var
$ du -sh /var/* | sort -h | tail -3
2.1G /var/lib
1.4G /var/cache
900M /var/log
$ ls /proc/2310/fd | wc -l ; grep 'open files' /proc/2310/limits
2217
Max open files  4096  4096  files

Logrotate ran last night and compressed old logs. Red herring: someone suspects inode exhaustion (df -i shows 3% used).
questions.promptHtml: Where did the space go and how do you recover without restarting?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Delete more files" or "extend the disk": du shows only 4 GB of files.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which process writes logs? Does logrotate use copytruncate or create with a reload signal? Is the fd count rising over days?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Truncate the deleted-but-open file through /proc/PID/fd/N.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) deleted files still held open by a process (space is freed only when the last fd closes); (b) big file in a mount shadowed by another mount; (c) inode exhaustion, ruled out.
  4. How I'd verify: lsof +L1 lists open files with link count 0:
java 2310 app 5w REG 8,2 97420000000 0 /var/log/app.log (deleted)

and ls -l /proc/2310/fd | grep deleted. 5. Root cause: logrotate removed app.log, but the app kept its descriptor and wrote 97 GB into the unlinked inode, invisible to du but counted by df. The fd count also shows a slow leak towards the 4096 limit. 6. Fix: Immediate: : > /proc/2310/fd/5 to truncate. Permanent: configure logrotate with a postrotate signal (kill -HUP/reopen) or copytruncate; raise nofile appropriately and find the fd leak (lsof -p groups).

lsof +L1
: > /proc/2310/fd/5      # frees space immediately, process keeps running
  1. Prevention: Alert on df usage and on ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l vs limit; test log rotation in staging.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not restarting the service in a production peak if truncation works; copytruncate can lose a few lines, which I accept for logs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does du disagree with df? -> du walks directory entries; df reports filesystem blocks, including unlinked-but-open files.
  • Same issue with Docker? -> Container logs and overlay layers fill the node; use log rotation options and ephemeral-storage limits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A database host showed 30 GB free in du and 0 free in df for days; the culprit was a deleted 28 GB trace file held by a sidecar.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes random files or resizes the disk.
  • Hire: finds deleted-open files with lsof and truncates via /proc.
  • Strong hire: fixes logrotate semantics, adds fd and disk monitoring, and checks for fd leaks.

questions.promptHtml: How do you read iostat -x output, and why can %util be misleading?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you understand queues and parallel devices rather than a single number.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I look at await (time a request spends queued plus serviced), aqu-sz (average queue length), request size and IOPS against the device or cloud limit. %util is just the fraction of time at least one request was in flight, so on NVMe or RAID, which serve many requests in parallel, 100% does not mean there is no headroom. Latency plus queue depth tell me saturation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
$ iostat -xz 1
Device  r/s   w/s   rkB/s  wkB/s   r_await w_await aqu-sz rareq-sz %util
nvme0n1 450  2900   7200  185000     0.9    18.4    53.2   16.0   99.8
  • Healthy latency: NVMe under 1 ms, SATA SSD 1 to 2 ms, HDD 5 to 15 ms, cloud network disk 1 to 5 ms.
  • IOPS = r/s + w/s; throughput = rkB/s + wkB/s. 10,000 IOPS of 4 KB is only 40 MB/s but may hit an IOPS cap.
  • Small rareq-sz/wareq-sz with high IOPS means random I/O.
  • Cloud limits: gp3 baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s; burst-credit volumes can run dry.
iostat -x -> which device is saturated -> iotop / pidstat -d -> which process -> strace/lsof -> which file

Per-process: iotop -oPa, pidstat -d 1. Latency histograms: biolatency-bpfcc, per-I/O: biosnoop-bpfcc. Demote a noisy job with ionice -c3.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating %util 100% as definitive on NVMe/RAID.
  • Ignoring request size and pattern.
  • Blaming the app when a backup shares the volume.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does await include? -> Queue time plus service time.
  2. Sequential vs random? -> Request size and rate: large sizes mean sequential; HDDs suffer on random.
  3. How do you prove the cloud limit? -> The cloud IOPS metric is flat at the provisioned value while latency rises.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "check %util". Senior: queue depth and latency, request size, device limits, and the path from device to process to file.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A volume at its provisioned IOPS made a database slow while %util looked identical to a healthy hour.

questions.contextHtml:
A Redis primary with 24 GB data on a 32 GB host works fine for weeks. Every day at 02:00, during BGSAVE, it gets OOM-killed or shows 2-second latency spikes. Excerpts:

$ dmesg -T | grep -i oom
Out of memory: Killed process 5120 (redis-server) total-vm: 31457280kB anon-rss: 29360128kB
$ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
[always] madvise never
$ redis-cli info persistence | grep -E 'fork|cow'
latest_fork_usec:2310000
$ vmstat 1
 so 12000 bi 8000  (during the fork)

Writes during the snapshot are about 40,000/s. Red herring: the team suspects a memory leak because the dump is "only 24 GB".
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure and fix it without losing durability.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add swap" or "increase the instance a bit". Both ignore copy-on-write amplification.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: vm.overcommit_memory setting? Is THP enabled? Write rate during snapshot? Is there a replica that can take the snapshot instead?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the snapshot on the primary or run it on a replica; set THP to madvise/never; ensure headroom.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) fork plus copy-on-write: each written page is duplicated while the child holds the snapshot; with THP the unit is 2 MB, so a tiny write copies 2 MB; (b) fork latency itself (page tables of 24 GB, 2.3 s latest_fork_usec); (c) leak, ruled out by a stable working set; (d) swapping (so high) makes it worse.
  4. How I'd verify: INFO persistence (fork time, current_cow_size), /proc/PID/smaps_rollup, grep AnonHugePages /proc/meminfo, dmesg OOM verdict.
  5. Root cause: After fork, parent and child share pages. Every write during the 2-minute snapshot copies a page; with THP and random writes nearly every huge page is touched, so memory approaches 2x the dataset (up to 48 GB) on a 32 GB host: OOM. The fork also stalls the single thread while page tables are copied, giving 2 s pauses.
  6. Fix: THP never/madvise (as Redis recommends), vm.overcommit_memory=1, headroom of 30 to 50% free RAM, take snapshots on a replica, smaller shards, use AOF with rewrite scheduling off-peak, and on virtualised hosts note fork cost is higher.
echo madvise > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
sysctl vm.overcommit_memory=1
  1. Prevention: Alert on latest_fork_usec, current_cow_size, memory headroom; load-test the snapshot at peak write rate.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Disabling persistence entirely risks data loss; adding swap just trades OOM for multi-second stalls.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does overcommit_memory=1 matter? -> Without it fork may fail when the kernel refuses to promise duplicate memory.
  • What does a replica snapshot cost? -> Another copy of data; replication must keep up.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The incident only appeared after a feature increased the write rate from 5k to 40k/s; the snapshot overlap quietly doubled memory.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suspects a leak; adds swap.
  • Hire: explains COW and THP with numbers.
  • Strong hire: replica snapshots, overcommit, headroom policy, fork-time monitoring and trade-offs.

questions.promptHtml: A service has high latency but CPU is only 15%. A CPU flame graph looks flat. What do you do next?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know that CPU profiles cannot see blocked time and what tools reveal it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A CPU flame graph only samples threads that are running, so time spent waiting on locks, I/O or a downstream never shows up. I would switch to off-CPU analysis: an off-CPU flame graph built with offcputime-bpfcc/bpftrace shows where threads block and for how long. Alongside it I'd check thread dumps, strace -c -T, futex activity and ss -ti for slow downstream calls.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
latency = on-CPU time + off-CPU time (lock waits, I/O, sleeps, scheduler queue)
CPU graph: samples at 99 Hz where threads are RUNNING
Off-CPU graph: stacks weighted by blocked time (kernel sched events)
sudo offcputime-bpfcc -df -p $(pgrep -f checkout.jar) 30 > out.stacks
./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl --color=io --countname=us < out.stacks > offcpu.svg
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_read { @s[tid] = nsecs; }
 tracepoint:syscalls:sys_exit_read /@s[tid]/ { @us[comm] = hist((nsecs-@s[tid])/1000); delete(@s[tid]); }'

Tools: async-profiler (Java, -e wall or lock mode), py-spy dump, Go pprof block/mutex profiles, jstack grouping by state, Parca/Pyroscope continuous profiling. Differential flame graphs compare before/after a deploy. eBPF and perf have about 1 to 3% overhead; strace and heavy tracers do not belong on a hot path.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Concluding "not our code" from a flat CPU graph.
  • Missing that a wait under a lock is one thread's issue but many threads' latency.
  • Off-CPU graphs include idle waiting threads; filter to request threads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to see run-queue delay? -> runqlat-bpfcc, PSI cpu.
  2. How to spot lock contention quickly? -> strace -c futex share, jstack with many BLOCKED threads, async-profiler lock mode.
  3. Wall-clock profiling? -> Samples all threads regardless of state; good for latency attribution.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "profile again, look closer". Senior: reasons about on-CPU vs off-CPU time, picks eBPF/async-profiler wall or lock mode, and keeps overhead safe.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "fast CPU profile" hid a connection-pool wait that produced 90% of the latency; the off-CPU graph pointed straight at HikariPool.getConnection.

questions.contextHtml:
After raising the worker count from 16 to 64 on a 16-core host to "use more parallelism", throughput fell 35% and p99 tripled. Observations:

$ vmstat 1
 r  b  swpd  free  si so  bi bo    in     cs us sy id wa
 9  0     0 4.1G   0  0   0  4 41000 310000 31 24 45  0
$ sudo strace -c -f -p 2310 -- sleep 5
% time  seconds  usecs/call  calls   errors syscall
 71.00  14.1     310         45500   18200  futex
 12.00   2.4     ...
$ perf top -p 2310
 18% [kernel] _raw_spin_lock    11% libc pthread_mutex_lock

Red herring: memory and disk are fine.
questions.promptHtml: Why did more workers make it slower and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Need more CPU" or "tune the OS". CPU is 45% idle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What shared state do workers lock (a cache, a log, a connection pool)? Did the change happen with any code change? Is the workload CPU-bound or I/O-bound?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back to 16 workers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a hot mutex with futex wait/wake storms; (b) false sharing or cache line bouncing (spin locks in kernel); (c) NUMA effects; (d) scheduler thrash from more threads than cores (cs 310k/s).
  4. How I'd verify: strace -c -f showing 71% futex with high error rate (EAGAIN = contended), perf top/perf record -g to find the lock owner function, Java jstack (many BLOCKED) or async-profiler -e lock, off-CPU flame graph, mpstat -P ALL for hot cores.
  5. Root cause: Threads serialise on one lock; with 64 threads on 16 cores each acquisition triggers futex sleep/wake and context switches (310k/s), sys time 24%, and the lock hold time lengthens when the holder is descheduled. Parallelism beyond the critical section's capacity only adds overhead (Amdahl's law).
  6. Fix: Short term: fewer workers (cores x small factor). Long term: shrink the critical section, shard the lock (striping), use lock-free or per-thread structures, batch updates, avoid logging under lock, and size pools by measured scaling curve.
  7. Prevention: Scalability test: throughput vs thread count; alert on cs and futex share; code review for shared mutable state.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not pinning threads or touching kernel tunables before fixing the lock; striping adds complexity, so only for the proven hot lock.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why are futex errors high? -> Contended attempts return EAGAIN/ETIMEDOUT before sleeping.
  • What if it was NUMA? -> Remote memory access shows as low IPC in perf stat; fix with affinity or per-node data.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A metrics library with a global lock was invoked on every request. Removing it from the hot path doubled throughput without touching any other code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: asks for more hardware or random tuning.
  • Hire: identifies futex contention with strace/perf and scales workers back.
  • Strong hire: Amdahl reasoning, lock striping, off-CPU/lock profiling and a scalability test.

questions.contextHtml:
Vague report: "API latency doubled since Tuesday, nothing was deployed." You have SSH to one of 12 identical VMs on a public cloud (8 vCPU each). Excerpts from the slow VM and a healthy one:

slow:  %Cpu(s): 31 us, 9 sy, 0 wa, 2 si, 18 st      load 6.1   (r=7)
good:  %Cpu(s): 33 us, 8 sy, 0 wa, 2 si,  0 st      load 5.9   (r=7)
$ mpstat -P ALL 1  (slow VM)  CPU3: %irq 0  %soft 96  (others normal)
$ cat /proc/interrupts | grep eth0
 CPU3: 41203018 ...   CPU0..2,4..7: ~1000 each
$ ss -ti dst 10.0.3.7   retrans:0/12  rtt:18/9

Red herring: application GC logs show normal pauses.
questions.promptHtml: What do you conclude and what is your plan, given only these symptoms?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Deploy a fix / restart the app." No deployment happened and the application is fine.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the problem on all VMs or a subset? Same host/instance type? Any cloud maintenance events? Is the traffic mix different?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drain/replace the slow VM from the load balancer (instances are cattle); autoscaling can replace it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) noisy neighbour: st 18% means the hypervisor gives the VM less CPU than it asked for; (b) NIC interrupts all landing on CPU3 (%soft 96%), single-core bottleneck; (c) network retransmits (12 retrans, modest); (d) GC, ruled out.
  4. How I'd verify: top/mpstat for st and per-CPU si, /proc/interrupts and /proc/softirqs (NET_RX), ethtool -l/-S eth0, ethtool -x RSS indirection, compare with the healthy VM, cloud console events for the instance.
  5. Root cause: Two overlapping infrastructure faults: CPU steal from a noisy host reduces effective compute (18% of cycles), and packet processing is concentrated on one core because RSS/IRQ affinity is not spread (single queue or irqbalance disabled), making CPU3 a bottleneck for the network path. Neither shows in the application.
  6. Fix: Short term: replace the instance (new host), restart irqbalance or set RPS/XPS and multiple queues (ethtool -L eth0 combined 8, echo ff > /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-0/rps_cpus). Long term: use instance types with dedicated or newer-generation NICs, spread IRQs by default in the image, alert on st and per-core softirq.
  7. Prevention: Fleet comparison dashboards (outlier detection per VM), alert on steal over 5%, golden image with tuned networking.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not tuning the app or JVM; not making kernel network changes on live hosts without a canary.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does one VM look slow but average load looks fine? -> Load average does not show steal or a single hot core.
  • Dedicated hosts? -> Remove noisy neighbours at higher cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: For a week one availability zone's latency was "mysteriously" 20% worse. A fleet-wide steal-time dashboard pointed at one host generation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts or tunes the app.
  • Hire: spots st and per-core softirq, compares hosts, replaces the VM.
  • Strong hire: explains RSS/IRQ affinity, fleet outlier analysis, and builds alerts.

questions.contextHtml: Postmortem review. At 14:02 checkout p99 went from 80 ms to 6 s with 4% timeouts, 10 minutes after a deploy. The first responder restarted all pods at 14:06, latency recovered for 3 minutes, then returned. At 14:11 a second responder disabled the recommendations feature flag and everything normalised by 14:13. Evidence collected: none from before the restart. Later analysis of one surviving pod's thread dump and a profile shows 58% of samples in Pattern$Branch.match under RecommendationService.rank(). Leadership asks: "Why did it take 11 minutes, and what should the team do differently?"
questions.promptHtml: Walk through what should have happened and which action items you would propose.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Be faster and restart sooner." It rewards guessing and destroys evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was a deploy correlation noticed in the first minute? Which dashboards existed? Who had permission to flip flags? Were thread dumps/profiles possible before restarting?
  2. Immediate mitigation (what should have happened): Correlate with the deploy and flip the feature flag or roll back within about 2 minutes; if restarting is considered, first capture a thread dump and a 30 s profile from one pod.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (at 14:03): CPU-bound user code (vmstat r=21 on 8 cores, us 86%), not disk (wa 0), not memory (no swap). Then: regex/hot loop in the new feature, GC storm (excluded by jstat), lock contention (excluded by few futex).
  4. How I'd verify: uptime, vmstat 1 3, top -H (many request threads hot), jstat -gcutil, async-profiler 30 s flame graph, perf stat (IPC 2.1 = real compute), strace -c (few syscalls), per-endpoint latency metrics.
  5. Root cause: The new feature compiled a regex per request and used a pattern vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking on long titles; every request thread burned CPU, saturating all 8 cores. Restarting only reset state; the same traffic hit the same code, hence a 3-minute recovery.
  6. Fix: Precompile the Pattern as static final, use a linear-time pattern (possessive quantifiers) or RE2-style engine, cap title length at 200 chars, add a per-request time budget; add a latency alert on the endpoint and a load test with adversarial inputs in the release checklist.
  7. Prevention: Canary deploys with automatic rollback on SLO burn; flag-first rollouts; a "capture before restart" runbook step (thread dump, perf, dmesg); alert on CPU saturation per service.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not blaming the responder; the process lacked guardrails. Not skipping the mitigation-versus-fix distinction in the timeline.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just add servers? -> Backtracking cost can grow exponentially with input; capacity cannot absorb it, and it hides the defect.
  • What does the industry precedent show? -> Large CDN outage from a regex with catastrophic backtracking drove a switch to linear-time engines plus CPU circuit breakers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's runbook said "restart first". After adding "snapshot first, then restart" they found two recurring leaks within a month because evidence finally existed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames individuals; wants faster restarts.
  • Hire: separates mitigation from fix, proposes capture-before-restart and a canary rollback.
  • Strong hire: evidence-based timeline using USE, concrete code fixes and process action items with owners, and a rollout/flag strategy.
